title: Moccasin: Efficient Tensor Rematerialization for Neural Networks

en.text: On the edge hardware that runs today's neural networks (phones, wearables, on-device accelerators), the first wall you hit is usually not compute but memory. On-chip memory is small, and the moment a model's intermediate tensors no longer fit, the system has to reach for much slower external memory, which drags down both inference and training.

A well-known way around this is tensor rematerialization: instead of keeping every intermediate tensor in memory, you recompute some of them on demand, trading extra compute for a lower peak memory footprint. The catch is that recomputation costs time. That turns the problem into a scheduling one: given a compute graph and a fixed memory budget, which tensors should you retain and which should you recompute so that total execution time is as small as possible while peak memory never exceeds the budget? In general this is a PSPACE-complete combinatorial optimization.

The leading prior method, Checkmate, casts this as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP). It is expressive, but its number of Boolean decision variables grows with the square of the node count, O(n²). Past a few hundred nodes the solver either times out or runs out of memory. Moccasin, the method introduced in this paper, changes the formulation rather than the solver: it describes each node's tensor lifetime with a handful of retention intervals, which cuts the count of discrete variables from quadratic to linear, O(n). On graphs with hundreds of nodes and thousands of edges, that makes it up to roughly an order of magnitude faster than Checkmate.

en.caption: Figure 1. Total duration increase versus solve time for both methods on a real-world compute graph with n = 442 nodes and m = 1247 edges, with the memory budget set to 80% of the peak memory of the rematerialization-free schedule. Moccasin (green) converges to a low-overhead solution within a few hundred seconds; Checkmate (blue) reaches comparable quality only around 2000 seconds.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14463
Why rematerialization is hard to solve at scale

Every node in a compute graph is one operator that produces an intermediate tensor. Keeping a tensor around saves the time you would otherwise spend recomputing it but costs memory; recomputing it saves memory but costs time. The memory budget is what turns this trade-off into a constrained optimization. Checkmate handles it by attaching a Boolean variable to the question "is this tensor resident in memory at this time step?" for every tensor and every step, which is where the O(n²) variables come from. The formulation works well on small and medium graphs, but the variable count explodes once the graph reaches a few hundred nodes, at which point the solver runs out of either time or memory.
The core idea: retention intervals

Moccasin's key observation is that over an entire execution, a tensor is actually resident in memory during only a few stretches of time. Rather than track a separate Boolean for every time step, describe those stretches directly as intervals.

en.caption: Figure 2. The retention-intervals formulation. The horizontal axis is time partitioned into discrete events, and each row is one node. An interval runs from a start event s to an end event e: its first event marks recomputing the node and writing its tensor to memory, and its end marks the tensor being freed. Node 1 uses two intervals (it is recomputed once); the others use a single interval.

en.text: Each node is allowed up to Cv intervals, and each interval is described by an integer start, an integer end, and a Boolean activity flag. The objective minimizes a weighted sum over the active compute events, with each node's execution time as its weight, which is exactly the extra runtime that recomputation adds. The memory budget is expressed with the constraint-programming cumulative constraint (tensor sizes as resource demands, the budget M as capacity), and the data dependencies between nodes are handled with the reservoir constraint. The whole model is handed to Google OR-Tools' CP-SAT solver. In the experiments the per-node interval cap Cv is fixed at 2, so the total number of integer variables is only O(Cn), linear in the graph size.
Shrinking the search space with stages
Moccasin also offers an optional variant that snaps interval start times onto stages carved out of an input topological ordering.

en.caption: Figure 4. Grouping events into stages. When an input topological ordering is enforced, the start of each node's first interval becomes a fixed value rather than a free variable, which shrinks the overall search space and speeds up the solve.

en.text: The paper's ablation shows that this topological-ordering restriction, while it slightly enlarges the variables' domains, substantially compresses the search space and makes the solve faster; and setting Cv as small as 2 costs almost nothing in solution quality.
Results: same quality, far less solve time

The authors compare the two methods on a family of random layered graphs, G1 through G4 (from 100 up to 1000 nodes, and up to 5875 edges), and on real-world compute graphs, with the memory budget set to 80% and 90% of the rematerialization-free peak memory.

en.caption: Table 1. Solve time on the random layered graphs at a memory budget of 80% of the initial peak memory. "Duration increase" is the extra execution time, as a percentage, that rematerialization adds relative to the no-rematerialization schedule; "—" means the method found no feasible solution within the time limit.

en.text: Two things stand out. First, on the graphs both methods can solve (G1 and G2), Moccasin's solution quality (duration increase) is essentially the same as Checkmate's, but it gets there several to more than ten times faster. Second, and more telling: once the graph grows to 500 and 1000 nodes, Checkmate finds no feasible solution within a three-hour limit and exits out of memory, whereas Moccasin still converges to a good solution, under 1% duration increase, in under an hour. The curves on the real-world graph in Figure 1 are the visual version of that order-of-magnitude gap.
Takeaway and boundaries

The lesson in Moccasin is a plain one: reformulating a problem to use fewer variables often changes what is solvable more than swapping in a stronger solver would. By expressing rematerialization decisions as a small set of retention intervals, Moccasin brings the discrete-variable count down from O(n²) to O(n), which lets it handle compute graphs that prior methods simply could not, up to about an order of magnitude faster, while holding the added runtime overhead under 5%.

It is worth being clear about the boundary. Moccasin optimizes the step that produces an execution sequence, and that step is hardware-agnostic: the resulting sequence can run on any CPU or GPU. But it currently models rematerialization only, and does not yet incorporate paging (temporarily writing intermediate data out to external memory); the authors list combining the two as future work. For anyone who has to plan memory for large models at compile time, Moccasin offers an option that scales further than what came before.

In practice, the payoff is largest exactly where the older approach breaks down. Planning compile-time memory for a large model, or fitting training and inference onto devices with limited on-chip or GPU memory, is precisely the regime of big compute graphs, and the bigger the graph the wider Moccasin's margin; on small graphs the two methods are comparable. What the reformulation really buys, then, is not a uniform speedup on every case but a larger set of problems that can be solved at all.

zh.text: 在手机、可穿戴设备、端侧加速器这类边缘硬件上跑神经网络，最先撞上的瓶颈往往不是算力，而是内存。片上内存容量有限，一旦放不下所有中间张量，就只能频繁访问速度慢得多的外部内存，直接拖慢推理和训练。

一个经典的应对办法是「张量重计算」（tensor rematerialization）：不把每个中间张量都存下来，而是在需要时重新算一遍，用额外的计算换取更低的峰值内存。问题在于，重算是要花时间的。于是就有了一个调度难题：给定一张计算图和固定的内存预算，到底该保留哪些张量、重算哪些张量，才能让总执行时间尽可能短，同时峰值内存始终不超预算？这在一般情况下是 PSPACE-complete 的组合优化问题。

此前的代表性方法 Checkmate 把它建模成一个混合整数线性规划（MILP），表达能力很强，但布尔决策变量的数量随节点数 n 呈平方级 O(n²) 增长。图一大，求解器要么超时、要么内存耗尽。本文提出的 Moccasin 换了一种建模思路：用「保留区间」（retention intervals）描述每个节点的张量生命周期，把离散变量的数量从平方级压到线性级 O(n)，从而在几百节点、上千条边的大图上，比 Checkmate 快最多约一个数量级。

zh.caption: 图1 在一张 n=442 个节点、m=1247 条边的真实计算图上，两种方法的「总时长增幅 vs. 求解时间」对比（内存预算设为无重计算时峰值内存的 80%）。Moccasin（绿色）在两三百秒内就收敛到低时长增幅的解，Checkmate（蓝色）要到约 2000 秒才给出同等质量的结果。

zh.text: 论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14463
为什么重计算问题在大图上这么难求解

计算图里每个节点对应一次算子计算，产出一个中间张量。保留张量能省下重算的时间，却要一直占着内存；重算能省内存，代价是多花时间。内存预算正是把这个取舍变成一个约束优化问题的关键。Checkmate 的做法，是给「某个张量在某个时间步是否驻留内存」这件事都配一个布尔变量，于是变量数量随节点数和时间步数一起膨胀，达到 O(n²) 量级。这套表达在中小规模的图上很有效，但一旦图长到几百个节点，变量数就会爆炸，求解随之失控。
方法核心：用「保留区间」描述张量生命周期
Moccasin 的关键观察是：在整个执行过程里，一个张量其实只会经历少数几段「待在内存里」的时间。与其为每个时间步单独记一个布尔量，不如直接用区间来刻画这些驻留段。

zh.caption: 图2 保留区间形式化的示意。横轴是被划分成「事件」（event）的时间，每一行对应一个节点。每段区间由一个起始事件 s 和一个结束事件 e 界定：区间的第一个事件表示重新计算该节点、把张量写入内存，区间结束表示张量被释放。图中节点 1 用了两段区间（说明它被重算了一次），其余节点各用一段。

zh.text: 每个节点最多允许 Cv 段区间，每段由整数起点、整数终点，以及一个布尔活跃标志描述。目标函数是最小化所有活跃计算事件的加权和，权重就是各节点的执行时间，也就是重算带来的总时长开销。内存预算用约束规划里的 cumulative 约束表达：把张量大小当作资源占用、把预算 M 当作容量；节点间的数据依赖则用 reservoir 约束刻画。整套模型交给 Google OR-Tools 的 CP-SAT 求解器求解。实验里把每个节点的区间上限 Cv 固定为 2，于是整数变量总数只有 O(Cn)，随图规模线性增长。
用「阶段」进一步收缩搜索空间
Moccasin 还提供一个可选变体：强制区间的起点对齐到按输入拓扑序划分出的「阶段」（stage）。

zh.caption: 图4 把事件按阶段分组的示意。当强制采用一个输入拓扑序时，每个节点第一段区间的起点被固定为定值，不再是自由变量，从而缩小整体搜索空间、加快求解。

zh.text: 论文的消融实验显示，这个拓扑序约束虽然会略微放大变量的取值域，却能显著压缩搜索空间，让求解更快；而把 Cv 压到 2 这么小，也几乎不损失解的质量。
实验结果：解的质量持平，求解时间大幅缩短
作者在一组随机分层图（random layered graphs）G1 到 G4（节点数从 100 到 1000，边数最多 5875）以及真实计算图上做了对比，内存预算取无重计算时峰值内存的 80% 和 90%。

zh.caption: 表1 随机分层图上的求解时间对比（内存预算为初始峰值内存的 80%）。「总时长增幅」指重计算方案相对无重计算方案增加的执行时间百分比；「—」表示方法在时限内未找到任何可行解。

zh.text: 可以看到两点。第一，在两种方法都能求解的图上（G1、G2），Moccasin 得到的解质量（总时长增幅）与 Checkmate 基本持平，但求解时间快了数倍到十几倍。第二，也是更关键的一点：当图长到 500、1000 个节点时，Checkmate 在三小时时限内找不到任何可行解、并因内存耗尽退出，而 Moccasin 仍能在一小时内收敛到总时长增幅低于 1% 的好解。值得一提的是，Moccasin 在整张表里给出的解，总时长增幅都稳定低于 1%，意味着为省内存而多付出的重算时间几乎可以忽略。图1 那张真实图上的曲线，正是这种数量级差距的直观写照。
小结与边界
Moccasin 的启示很朴素：换一个更省变量的问题建模，往往比换一个更强的求解器更能改变「什么规模可解」。把重计算决策表达成少量保留区间，让离散变量从 O(n²) 降到 O(n)，Moccasin 就能处理此前方法根本啃不动的大计算图，求解速度最高快约一个数量级，同时把重计算带来的额外运行时开销始终压在 5% 以内，几乎不影响整体的执行效率。
也需要说明边界：这套方法优化的是「求解出执行序列」这一步，本身与硬件无关，解出来的序列可以在任意 CPU 或 GPU 上执行；但它目前只考虑重计算，尚未纳入「换页」（paging，把中间数据临时写到外部内存）这类策略，作者把与换页结合列为后续工作。对需要在编译期为大模型做内存规划的场景，Moccasin 提供了一个更能向大图扩展的选项。
落到工程实践上，收益最大的地方，恰恰是老方法失效的地方。为大模型做编译期内存规划，或者把训练与推理塞进显存、片上内存受限的设备，正是「大计算图」这一档：图越大，Moccasin 相对以往方法的优势越明显，而在小图上两者差距并不大。所以这套重新建模真正换来的，不是对每个案例都提速，而是把「根本能不能解」的边界往外推了一大截。

en.title: ICML 2023: Making Tensor Rematerialization Scale by Making the Problem Smaller
en.subtitle: Moccasin, from Qualcomm AI Research and USC, recasts rematerialization as a constraint program with a linear rather than quadratic number of decision variables

zh.title: ICML 2023 | 把张量重计算问题「变小」，Moccasin 让大计算图求解快一个数量级
zh.subtitle: Qualcomm AI Research 与南加州大学提出基于约束规划的张量重计算新形式，把离散决策变量从平方级压到线性级

en.text: On the edge hardware that runs today's neural networks (phones, wearables, on-device accelerators), the first wall you hit is usually not compute but memory. On-chip memory is small, and the moment a model's intermediate tensors no longer fit, the system has to reach for much slower external memory, which drags down both inference and training.

A well-known way around this is tensor rematerialization: instead of keeping every intermediate tensor in memory, you recompute some of them on demand, trading extra compute for a lower peak memory footprint. The catch is that recomputation costs time. That turns the problem into a scheduling one: given a compute graph and a fixed memory budget, which tensors should you retain and which should you recompute so that total execution time is as small as possible while peak memory never exceeds the budget? In general this is a PSPACE-complete combinatorial optimization.

The leading prior method, Checkmate, casts this as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP). It is expressive, but its number of Boolean decision variables grows with the square of the node count, O(n²). Past a few hundred nodes the solver either times out or runs out of memory. Moccasin, the method introduced in this paper, changes the formulation rather than the solver: it describes each node's tensor lifetime with a handful of retention intervals, which cuts the count of discrete variables from quadratic to linear, O(n). On graphs with hundreds of nodes and thousands of edges, that makes it up to roughly an order of magnitude faster than Checkmate.

en.caption: Figure 1. Total duration increase versus solve time for both methods on a real-world compute graph with n = 442 nodes and m = 1247 edges, with the memory budget set to 80% of the peak memory of the rematerialization-free schedule. Moccasin (green) converges to a low-overhead solution within a few hundred seconds; Checkmate (blue) reaches comparable quality only around 2000 seconds.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14463
Takeaway and boundaries

The lesson in Moccasin is a plain one: reformulating a problem to use fewer variables often changes what is solvable more than swapping in a stronger solver would. By expressing rematerialization decisions as a small set of retention intervals, Moccasin brings the discrete-variable count down from O(n²) to O(n), which lets it handle compute graphs that prior methods simply could not, up to about an order of magnitude faster, while holding the added runtime overhead under 5%.

It is worth being clear about the boundary. Moccasin optimizes the step that produces an execution sequence, and that step is hardware-agnostic: the resulting sequence can run on any CPU or GPU. But it currently models rematerialization only, and does not yet incorporate paging (temporarily writing intermediate data out to external memory); the authors list combining the two as future work. For anyone who has to plan memory for large models at compile time, Moccasin offers an option that scales further than what came before.

In practice, the payoff is largest exactly where the older approach breaks down. Planning compile-time memory for a large model, or fitting training and inference onto devices with limited on-chip or GPU memory, is precisely the regime of big compute graphs, and the bigger the graph the wider Moccasin's margin; on small graphs the two methods are comparable. What the reformulation really buys, then, is not a uniform speedup on every case but a larger set of problems that can be solved at all.

en.caption: Figure 1. Total duration increase versus solve time for both methods on a real-world compute graph with n = 442 nodes and m = 1247 edges, with the memory budget set to 80% of the peak memory of the rematerialization-free schedule. Moccasin (green) converges to a low-overhead solution within a few hundred seconds; Checkmate (blue) reaches comparable quality only around 2000 seconds.

en.text: Results: same quality, far less solve time

The authors compare the two methods on a family of random layered graphs, G1 through G4 (from 100 up to 1000 nodes, and up to 5875 edges), and on real-world compute graphs, with the memory budget set to 80% and 90% of the rematerialization-free peak memory.

en.caption: Table 1. Solve time on the random layered graphs at a memory budget of 80% of the initial peak memory. "Duration increase" is the extra execution time, as a percentage, that rematerialization adds relative to the no-rematerialization schedule; "—" means the method found no feasible solution within the time limit.

en.text: Two things stand out. First, on the graphs both methods can solve (G1 and G2), Moccasin's solution quality (duration increase) is essentially the same as Checkmate's, but it gets there several to more than ten times faster. Second, and more telling: once the graph grows to 500 and 1000 nodes, Checkmate finds no feasible solution within a three-hour limit and exits out of memory, whereas Moccasin still converges to a good solution, under 1% duration increase, in under an hour. The curves on the real-world graph in Figure 1 are the visual version of that order-of-magnitude gap.

zh.caption: 图1 在一张 n=442 个节点、m=1247 条边的真实计算图上，两种方法的「总时长增幅 vs. 求解时间」对比（内存预算设为无重计算时峰值内存的 80%）。Moccasin（绿色）在两三百秒内就收敛到低时长增幅的解，Checkmate（蓝色）要到约 2000 秒才给出同等质量的结果。

zh.text: 实验结果：解的质量持平，求解时间大幅缩短
作者在一组随机分层图（random layered graphs）G1 到 G4（节点数从 100 到 1000，边数最多 5875）以及真实计算图上做了对比，内存预算取无重计算时峰值内存的 80% 和 90%。

zh.caption: 表1 随机分层图上的求解时间对比（内存预算为初始峰值内存的 80%）。「总时长增幅」指重计算方案相对无重计算方案增加的执行时间百分比；「—」表示方法在时限内未找到任何可行解。

zh.text: 可以看到两点。第一，在两种方法都能求解的图上（G1、G2），Moccasin 得到的解质量（总时长增幅）与 Checkmate 基本持平，但求解时间快了数倍到十几倍。第二，也是更关键的一点：当图长到 500、1000 个节点时，Checkmate 在三小时时限内找不到任何可行解、并因内存耗尽退出，而 Moccasin 仍能在一小时内收敛到总时长增幅低于 1% 的好解。值得一提的是，Moccasin 在整张表里给出的解，总时长增幅都稳定低于 1%，意味着为省内存而多付出的重算时间几乎可以忽略。图1 那张真实图上的曲线，正是这种数量级差距的直观写照。

zh.subtitle: Qualcomm AI Research 与南加州大学提出基于约束规划的张量重计算新形式，把离散决策变量从平方级压到线性级

en.caption: Figure 4. Grouping events into stages. When an input topological ordering is enforced, the start of each node's first interval becomes a fixed value rather than a free variable, which shrinks the overall search space and speeds up the solve.

en.text: Why rematerialization is hard to solve at scale

Every node in a compute graph is one operator that produces an intermediate tensor. Keeping a tensor around saves the time you would otherwise spend recomputing it but costs memory; recomputing it saves memory but costs time. The memory budget is what turns this trade-off into a constrained optimization. Checkmate handles it by attaching a Boolean variable to the question "is this tensor resident in memory at this time step?" for every tensor and every step, which is where the O(n²) variables come from. The formulation works well on small and medium graphs, but the variable count explodes once the graph reaches a few hundred nodes, at which point the solver runs out of either time or memory.

zh.text: 用「阶段」进一步收缩搜索空间
Moccasin 还提供一个可选变体：强制区间的起点对齐到按输入拓扑序划分出的「阶段」（stage）。

zh.caption: 图4 把事件按阶段分组的示意。当强制采用一个输入拓扑序时，每个节点第一段区间的起点被固定为定值，不再是自由变量，从而缩小整体搜索空间、加快求解。

zh.text: 论文的消融实验显示，这个拓扑序约束虽然会略微放大变量的取值域，却能显著压缩搜索空间，让求解更快；而把 Cv 压到 2 这么小，也几乎不损失解的质量。

zh.text: 小结与边界
Moccasin 的启示很朴素：换一个更省变量的问题建模，往往比换一个更强的求解器更能改变「什么规模可解」。把重计算决策表达成少量保留区间，让离散变量从 O(n²) 降到 O(n)，Moccasin 就能处理此前方法根本啃不动的大计算图，求解速度最高快约一个数量级，同时把重计算带来的额外运行时开销始终压在 5% 以内，几乎不影响整体的执行效率。
也需要说明边界：这套方法优化的是「求解出执行序列」这一步，本身与硬件无关，解出来的序列可以在任意 CPU 或 GPU 上执行；但它目前只考虑重计算，尚未纳入「换页」（paging，把中间数据临时写到外部内存）这类策略，作者把与换页结合列为后续工作。对需要在编译期为大模型做内存规划的场景，Moccasin 提供了一个更能向大图扩展的选项。
落到工程实践上，收益最大的地方，恰恰是老方法失效的地方。为大模型做编译期内存规划，或者把训练与推理塞进显存、片上内存受限的设备，正是「大计算图」这一档：图越大，Moccasin 相对以往方法的优势越明显，而在小图上两者差距并不大。所以这套重新建模真正换来的，不是对每个案例都提速，而是把「根本能不能解」的边界往外推了一大截。

en.caption: Figure 1. Total duration increase versus solve time for both methods on a real-world compute graph with n = 442 nodes and m = 1247 edges, with the memory budget set to 80% of the peak memory of the rematerialization-free schedule. Moccasin (green) converges to a low-overhead solution within a few hundred seconds; Checkmate (blue) reaches comparable quality only around 2000 seconds.

en.text: Takeaway and boundaries

The lesson in Moccasin is a plain one: reformulating a problem to use fewer variables often changes what is solvable more than swapping in a stronger solver would. By expressing rematerialization decisions as a small set of retention intervals, Moccasin brings the discrete-variable count down from O(n²) to O(n), which lets it handle compute graphs that prior methods simply could not, up to about an order of magnitude faster, while holding the added runtime overhead under 5%.

It is worth being clear about the boundary. Moccasin optimizes the step that produces an execution sequence, and that step is hardware-agnostic: the resulting sequence can run on any CPU or GPU. But it currently models rematerialization only, and does not yet incorporate paging (temporarily writing intermediate data out to external memory); the authors list combining the two as future work. For anyone who has to plan memory for large models at compile time, Moccasin offers an option that scales further than what came before.

In practice, the payoff is largest exactly where the older approach breaks down. Planning compile-time memory for a large model, or fitting training and inference onto devices with limited on-chip or GPU memory, is precisely the regime of big compute graphs, and the bigger the graph the wider Moccasin's margin; on small graphs the two methods are comparable. What the reformulation really buys, then, is not a uniform speedup on every case but a larger set of problems that can be solved at all.
